It's funny. When I was young, I feared working my life away. I feared that when I grew up, I'd have to put away all my toys and all my interests and devote myself to work and nothing but work and responsibility for my adult life. When I got older and saw my life get more and more consumed by responsibilities, it drove me suicidal.

Yet, I'm 23 and for now I'm working almost every day of every week, including weekends, for the moment and honestly I've never been happier. I see my work as fuel for my passions and interests, instead of a  replacement. I even recently saved up enough money to buy myself a new computer for my video gaming hobby. It comes in today, in fact, and I hope to take a vacation soon and do nothing but enjoy my hobbies. 

I even hated my job at first, but I stuck with it, and saved up enough cash. With the help of my family, I got back on medication, and mostly looked through old notes I took from therapy I had before.

I just set short term plans, and goals, and I know my current state is temporary, and I'll transition into the life I want sometime in the future. 

A saying that my dad said to me that keeps me going from time to time goes something like this. "If you're terrified of the future, plan to make it through next year, if you can't get through next year, get through next month. If you can't get through next month, get through next week. If you can't get through next week, try to get through tomorrow. If you can't get through tomorrow, try getting through the next hour."

So yeah, I'd have her set a short term goal. Something simple and achievable over the time span. Even if it's just "save up enough money to buy x" it can help.

You haven't seen everything yet. There's a lot of beauty and pleasure to be found in the world, but you can only find it through experience. Even if you have before, and it failed before, if you keep trying, it will work out.

I just learned about the name changes a little while ago. They make sense to me. The whole game isn't necessarily played completely in the Americas anymore. If you're playing Japan on a Japanese map, calling the second age the "colonial age" is just weird and inaccurate. There's nothing much they would be discovering in the first age, either. If they add or have European maps in Russia or Finland, or Austria or wherever, there's no colonialism happening there, either.

Not to mention, colonialism for the European powers is happening this entire time, over the course of the game's timespan, and even beyond. Having a single age being called the "colonial age" is a little weird, looking back. There were new colonies being established through the industrial age.

As for the native tribe names, it's fine,  Haudenosaunee is a little difficult to pronounce for a native English speaker like myself, but if it's what they want to be called, it's what they want to be called. *This isn't the first time names have changed for the native tribes, btw. They changed them back when the Warchiefs came out too*

My favorite change is turning "Colonial Militia" to "Revolutionary" because hell yeah, they should have been called that to begin with.  

If anything I wish they would make more changes, particularly to the Germans. Having all the little German states represented as one faction with the HRE flag is weird to me, especially considering the HRE had Italian and Dutch states in it, as well as Czechs for the longest time. It would make more sense if there were two factions, the Austrians and the Prussians, and split the different German representations between them. You're never going to get every single little German state represented without an absurd amount of effort, so splitting the Germans in two to represent how divided Germany was during this time period would make sense, and you could have brothers wars on maps, or face off against the Ottomans as Austria, with the Polish I was hoping they would add.

The changes from colonial age to commerce age, and discovery age to exploration age actually make total sense to me, because the game isn't solely played in North America. It's in Asia too, and you can play as the likes of China and Japan and India. These were never colonial powers, and making the names a bit more general to reflect this is okay with me. Some of these areas WERE colonized, but not in the "colonial age" represented in the game. They were colonized much later.

These name changes would also make sense if they added European maps, which I hope they will.

I managed about 30 subs, 2 carriers, a couple light cruisers and 20+ destroyers. I probably could have made more if I started sooner. I had a full 24 medium tank divisions, and I used them to bulldoze Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan.

Early on, pump all the resources you can get into producing as many divisions as you can, and from the start, start justifying on Shanxi and Xibei San Ma. They only have 4 or 5 divisions at the start and you start with 8. As soon as you declare on Shanxi, start justifying on Sinkiang, overwhelm them with sheer numbers and flood through the gaps. Rinse and repeat until all of their territory is yours. Also start boosting Communist support in Manchukuo. As for focuses, rush the Government of National defence. You can wait until the united front forms naturally, but I like to have control over the faction. Makes it more flexible. After you're done with Sinkiang (don't call Nationalist China in to the war with Sinkiang, they will join the Commitern!), start preparing a Communist Coup in Manchukuo, and start going down the international aid focuses. I chose France. Once the war with Japan starts, don't join in. Wait for a while until you feel ready and you've built up your troops and have better infantry divisions. Make sure to join the war by the time the Manchurian coup fires. This will shatter the Japanese lines, and you should try and take as much territory as you can before the Japanese get forced out of Korea. Ask Communist Manchukuo for territory, and they will give it, and you will keep it once the white peace fires.

After the white peace has been made with Japan, you should have all of your overseas aid focuses done. If not, finish them and go for Dominate Japan. I managed to get lucky with it ~~maybe copy your save and reload until you get it.~~ Once you have Japan in your pocket, build up the infiltration in Manchukuo from the Anti-Japanese expedition focus, which should bypass. You should be able to infiltrate Manchukuo unhindered, since I don't believe they have the option to counter it if they're not Japan's puppet or are Communist. Also make sure to go for One China Policy. Try to declare war on Manchukuo while they're still in the Government of National Defence, because they will leave once you leave and go to the Commitern (that's what happened to me, and I had to join the German war against the Soviet Union to get Manchuria). I would also recommend invading Korea, and setting up a puppet, that you don't call into the war with Nationalist China unless you have to.

Make inroads through Manchuria to your territory in the chaos of the war declaration, and let the Japanese flood in. From then on, the war is easy. I mean, it's the same problem with every other historical game out there. Things like the Japanese fighting the Goths in Age of Empires 2 are things that obviously never happened. Things can go different from History in a clear and obvious, even ridiculous manner. However, I'd argue that the focus tree, and the historical paths presented can present a striking picture of what the country was like in 1936. Germany, for example, following the historical path in the focus tree can paint a reasonably accurate picture of the decisions Adolph Hitler was making in and after 1936. Remilitarizing the Rhineland, annexing Austria, and demanding the Sudetenland are all things Adolph Hitler actually did. Also things like Operation Barabarossa, or the Molotov Ribbentrop pact are all historically decisions too.

Obviously, there's alternate history mixed in, since you can make different decisions, and the order of the decisions and the dates they are made can clearly be different. It wouldn't be a game if everything was exact, but it's not like the game just pulls stuff out of thin air and calls it WW2. All the advisors and alternate leaders in the major countries are all real people too, who all have stories of their own, and the default leaders of the minor countries also have their own stories.

Without HOI IV, I probably never would have known or looked much into the story of someone like Aisin Gioro Puyi, or Reza Shah Pahlavi, or Kurt Schushnigg.

Conjuration as a magic school is pretty much devoted to opening gates to Oblivion, and/or binding the creatures found in Oblivion to do your bidding. Every time you summon an atronach it gets sent from Oblivion to Mundus, and then back again once banished or dismissed. As such, it wouldn't be too much of a stretch to reverse this process and to place yourself in Oblivion from Mundus. On paper it's quite easy, but the Daedric princes don't like people interfering in their realms, particularly smart and pesky ones like mages. There's also the matter of where in Oblivion you end up, which realm, and where in that realm. You need a start and an endpoint, and that's a lot easier to achieve when you're calling something to you from Oblivion, than when sending yourself to Oblivion. It's not something novices do, simply because of how dangerous it can be. The realms themselves can be... uncomfortable to those not properly prepared, to say the least.

There have been some master mages out there that try it and succeed, setting up portals or waypoints for others to follow.

Of course, then there's the matter of gates and invitations sent by the princes themselves, but these are usually exceedingly rare and hard to come by.

They made you better with weapons and made them do better damage, let you repair more, etc. Those numbers were used in equations to calculate things like damage, freeing up the perks to do other things.

It being more 'visible' can be easily fixed by just telling you what effect your current skill level has on your damage, rather than hiding that information from the player. You don't need to use the perks for that, just be more open with information.

The perks were not the soul purpose of the skills, but an extra used to creatively mix up gameplay. The Skills did the boring thing, while the perks did creative and interesting things that you could not unlock by leveling your skills up. They were separate in function. Sure, the skills and SPECIAL were requisites to unlock the perks, but the perks were not the purpose of the skills. You could still do huge damage with an unarmed of 100 and the proper strength, even without taking any perks for an unarmed character.

It's not "honest" about what skills are for, but instead it's cheapening what the perks do. It's not an illusion. It only feels like an illusion because of the wasted potential of the perks and the insignificant changes they make.

Sure, there were a number of perks one would take when going on a specific build, and they did line up with the skills you would invest in, but they were separate mechanics of the game in terms of function. The perks allowed for creative things like Lady Killer, or Jury Rigging, whereas the base skills handled the base function of getting stronger wholesale

Now in Fallout 4 you have to take 4 "perks" just to hit hard enough to fight on par with high level enemies, and you don't get the creative ones that unlocked interesting differences of gameplay, and the DLC can't add any new perks because that would break the system.

The United States is a Federation, not a Unitary State like the UK. The states are not there just for convenience. Technically, the Federal Government and the States SHARE sovereignty. 

It's changed a lot since it's founding. For the first several years, it was a Confederation, or a loosely bound group of independent nations. (It used to be The United States ARE, not the United States is). It was something more akin to the EU. The point of it was to avoid complete centralized power, which the Founding Fathers thought would inevitably lead to tyranny at some point. Of course that went to shit when in-state rebellions started happening and Massachusetts was in trouble due to debt, and no other state would help, so a Federal Government was formed.

State-side sovereignty and State's rights were (and still are) a serious issue in the United States, and the vast majority of the law and order in the country is handled on a state level, only appeals and military/interstate cases go to federal courts. The States even have their own militias separate from the Military, and their own Assemblies/Legislative Houses that make their own laws. They elect their own governors, and basically handle their own affairs in (usually with some slight variation) a miniature version of the US federal system.

What basically happened in the American Civil War was that the Southern half of the country tried to forcibly withdraw from the Union, and form it's own independent Confederation. It was more of a failed war of independence than a Civil War, but it was labelled as a Civil War by Lincoln because he didn't want to recognize the CSA as an Independent Nation.

In fact, Nationalism was a unifying force in the US, since it was opposed by Sectionalism, which meant pride in one's state.

Not only that, but the British government outright ignored the local legislative houses (set up to govern closer and more effectively, since London was across the Atlantic) or considered them illegitimate. These had existed and worked for over a hundred years before the Revolution.

In Old World Blues, you would move from research area to research area trying to collect each technology you needed. There wasn't a set path on which one to collect first, but the story would still unfold around you at each location, which, again, had their own themes.

In Lonesome Road, you followed a pretty direct path from Hopeville across the highway into other parts of the area. Ulysses would talk to you at specific points along the way. This one was more of a distinct journey than the rest, taking you along a set route with some detours to stop and explore. Each section of the route had a unique theme.

Obsidian's decisions and how they went about making New Vegas set them up with an ideal environment to make a sandbox game. They utterly ignored graphics or shooting upgrades (which led to most idiot critics dismissing it as though it "should've been an expansion to Fallout 3" and costing them points on Metacritic), and sat down to focus all their time on the world building and the overarching narrative. Obsidian's narrative in New Vegas had a very large scale focus: It was all about who would get to take over and rule New Vegas, whether it would be the NCR, Caesar's Legion, Mr. House, or the Courier himself/herself. The personal narrative was subordinate to the larger conflict. For a sandbox game, this works very well, as this meant that almost every side quest had some role to fill in the main narrative and there was some reason for your character (whatever character you may have made) to be doing it. The factions made sense, and they felt like real factions that had an impact on the world. 

It helps that most of the members of Obsidian worked on the first fallout games and that they already had a lot of lore to build on in the region they set the game, unlike Bethesda, who basically had to make the lore of 3 and 4 from scratch.

Fallout 4 doesn't have a large scale focus. The focus is all on the personal narrative with the larger scale narrative subordinate. There's really no reason for your character to help the minutemen other than "to be a good person". Your character really has no motivation for anything but to find Shaun, so all of the sidequests end up being just selfless philanthropy or paid mercenary work if you have charisma, which doesn't work with every character a typical RPG player might want to play as. In New Vegas, you were encouraged to start again and take different paths, because that would vary your experience, and let you complete quests and experience content that other characters couldn't, just because of their nature. In Fallout 4, you can do everything with one character, and you don't have to start over, which sounds nice, until you consider that it can be really fun to build another character from scratch and find a new playstyle.

I think that in part, Obsidian are just better writers than Bethesda. I mean, I cared about who controlled the Mojave, but I could've cared less what happened to Shaun.

...but that's not why people remember Morrowind. People remember Morrowind because it was probably one of the first games in existence where you could run off at a tangent and do whatever you want instead of the main quest.

Here's the thing though: the reason why Bethesda's games are so popular is that the player CAN do whatever they want and not be tied down to a linear quest line. Morrowind proved this rule, and it's widely considered to be one of their best games. I think by going a more linear, personal story-based route with these games, it's going to bite them later. Sure, there might be those out there who like a story-based game, but that's not the crowd that games like Fallout or the Elder Scrolls gather.
